lead: A closure of a relation is the smallest new relation that has one property the original lacks. It keeps every original pair and adds only the pairs forced by the property. Reflexive, symmetric and transitive closures answer three different questions. The transitive closure is the expensive one: it asks which vertices are reachable from which. Warshall's algorithm computes it on a 0-1 matrix in n³ small Boolean steps, with no recursion and no path search. Network reachability, task dependencies and database joins all use this idea.
prereq: You need Chapter 2.2 for the 0-1 matrix, the digraph and the definition of transitivity.

blocks.text: Let R be a relation on a finite set A. The reflexive closure of R is R ∪ Δ, where Δ = {(a,a) : a ∈ A} is the diagonal relation. It adds a self-loop at every vertex that lacks one. The symmetric closure is R ∪ R⁻¹, where R⁻¹ = {(b,a) : (a,b) ∈ R}. It adds the reverse of every arrow.

blocks.where: R is the relation; Δ is the diagonal {(a,a) : a ∈ A}.
R⁻¹ is the inverse relation, every pair reversed.

blocks.text: The transitive closure is the expensive one. A pair (a,b) belongs to R⁺ when A has a path a = v₀ → v₁ → … → v<sub>m</sub> = b of length m ≥ 1 with every step in R. Equivalently, (a,b) ∈ R⁺ if and only if (a,b) ∈ R<sup>m</sup> for some m ≥ 1. For a set of n elements, R⁺ = R ∪ R² ∪ R³ ∪ … ∪ Rⁿ.

Powers above n add no new pairs. A path with more than n edges repeats an internal vertex, and cutting the cycle shortens it without changing the endpoints. One case needs the full n: a simple cycle of length n is the shortest non-empty path from a vertex back to itself, so (a,a) can first appear in Rⁿ. That is why the union runs to Rⁿ and not to R<sup>n−1</sup>. For two distinct endpoints a ≠ b, a simple path uses at most n−1 edges.

Write R* = R⁺ ∪ Δ. This is the connectivity relation: (a,b) ∈ R* means b is reachable from a by a path of length zero or more. Length zero is the case a = b, which is why R* is always reflexive. R⁺ need not be reflexive.
Number the elements 1 to n. Store the relation in a Boolean matrix W, where W[i][j] = 1 when (i,j) ∈ R and 0 otherwise. Warshall adds vertices to a permitted intermediate set one at a time.

items: Start with W equal to the relation matrix. Think of k = 0: no vertex may be used as a stepping stone.
For k = 1 to n, run over every row i and column j.
Set W[i][j] = W[i][j] OR (W[i][k] AND W[k][j]).
After the pass for k, W[i][j] = 1 exactly when a path from i to j uses only intermediate vertices from {1, 2, …, k}.

blocks.where: i is the start row; j is the end column; k is the vertex allowed as a stepping stone; ∨ is OR; ∧ is AND.

blocks.text: The order matters for the proof, not for the final answer. When k is processed, W[i][k] and W[k][j] already describe paths through {1, …, k−1}. Chaining them gives a path through {1, …, k}. A path that avoids k was already present. So after pass k, W[i][j] = 1 exactly when a path from i to j uses only intermediate vertices from {1, …, k}.
Three nested loops, each running n times, give O(n³) Boolean operations. Memory is O(n²). There is no recursion and no queue; the matrix is the whole state.

Warshall answers reachability: can I get from i to j? That is the same question as connectivity in a directed graph. Unit 6 reuses the idea for graph connectivity and for shortest-path algorithms. A database join can be planned by closing a relation of table links. A build system can close a relation of depends on.

Other methods exist. Cumulative squaring starts with S = I ∨ R, where I is the identity matrix, then repeats S ← S ∨ S² until S stops changing; each round folds in every power up to double the previous limit, so no odd power is skipped. Binary exponentiation of I ∨ R does the same job in fewer multiplications. Both are polynomial, and both are easy to get wrong by hand. A depth-first search from every vertex finds reachability in O(n(n + m)) for a graph with m edges, which beats O(n³) on sparse graphs. Warshall wins when the relation is dense or already a matrix.
Transitive reduction is the opposite job: remove edges that the transitive closure can rebuild. The name is enough here.

figure.caption: Each pass lets one more vertex act as a stepping stone; by k = 3, vertex 1 reaches 2, 3 and 4.

examples.question: Let A = {1,2,3,4} and R = {(1,2),(2,3),(3,4),(4,2)}. (a) Write the reflexive closure and the symmetric closure, listing every added pair. (b) Find the transitive closure R⁺ by listing all pairs and by running Warshall's algorithm. (c) Give row 1 of the matrix after each k = 0,1,2,3,4.
steps: Reflexive closure: Δ = {(1,1),(2,2),(3,3),(4,4)}. None is in R, so add all four. R<sub>ref</sub> = R ∪ Δ.
Symmetric closure: R⁻¹ = {(2,1),(3,2),(4,3),(2,4)}. None is in R, so add these four. R<sub>sym</sub> = R ∪ R⁻¹.

Warshall matrix row 1: start W⁰ row 1 = 0 1 0 0. k=1: vertex 1 has no incoming edge, so no change: 0 1 0 0. k=2: W[1][3] becomes 1 because 1→2 and 2→3; row = 0 1 1 0. k=3: W[1][4] becomes 1 because 1→3 and 3→4; row = 0 1 1 1. k=4: no new 1 in row 1; row = 0 1 1 1.
The final row matches the pair list: 1 reaches 2,3,4 and not 1.
examples.answer: Reflexive closure adds 4 pairs; symmetric closure adds 4 pairs; R⁺ has 12 pairs, namely (1,2),(1,3),(1,4) plus all 9 pairs among {2,3,4}. Row 1 after k=0,1,2,3,4 is 0 1 0 0; 0 1 0 0; 0 1 1 0; 0 1 1 1; 0 1 1 1.
examples.check:
R = {(1,2),(2,3),(3,4),(4,2)}
A = [1,2,3,4]
ref_add = len({(a,a) for a in A} - R)
sym_add = len({(b,a) for (a,b) in R} - R)
n = 4
W = [[0]*n for _ in range(n)]
for (a,b) in R:
    W[a-1][b-1] = 1
for k in range(n):
    for i in range(n):
        for j in range(n):
            W[i][j] = W[i][j] or (W[i][k] and W[k][j])
trans = sum(sum(row) for row in W)
print(ref_add)
print(sym_add)
print(trans)
print(*W[0])

traps: Treating k as a start or end vertex. In Warshall, k is only an allowed intermediate vertex; the start i and the end j may be equal or different, and neither is replaced by k.

Stopping the union too early, say at R². Powers up to Rⁿ are needed: cutting a repeated vertex shortens long paths, but a simple cycle of length n is the shortest non-empty path from a vertex back to itself, so a self-pair can first appear in Rⁿ. Two distinct endpoints are joined by a simple path of at most n−1 edges, but self-pairs spoiling that bound is exactly why the union runs to Rⁿ.
Confusing R⁺ with R*. R⁺ uses paths of length at least 1 and need not be reflexive; R* adds Δ and is always reflexive.

Adding (a,a) in the transitive closure because a cycle exists somewhere else in the relation. Add (a,a) only when a non-empty path leads from a back to a. A vertex lying on a cycle of length 2 or more does get its self-loop, because the rest of the cycle is a path from a back to a.
Forgetting that the symmetric closure of a transitive relation can destroy transitivity; closures are taken one property at a time.

quiz.q: Define the reflexive closure of a relation R on a set A.
quiz.a: R ∪ Δ, where Δ = {(a,a) : a ∈ A}.

quiz.q: Why does R⁺ = R ∪ R² ∪ … ∪ Rⁿ stop at n for a set with n elements?
quiz.a: Any path with more than n−1 edges repeats a vertex. Removing the cycle gives a shorter path with the same endpoints, so no pair needs a power above n. The bound n, not n−1, is needed because a cycle of length n is the shortest non-empty path from a vertex back to itself.

quiz.q: For R = {(1,2),(2,3),(3,1)} on {1,2,3}, what is row 1 after Warshall's algorithm finishes?
quiz.a: All three entries are 1: 1→2→3→1, so vertex 1 reaches 1, 2 and 3.

quiz.q: Warshall's test uses W[i][k] AND W[k][j]. Explain why it is not W[k][i] AND W[j][k].
quiz.a: W[i][k] is a path i→k and W[k][j] is a path k→j; joined, they give i→k→j, a path from i to j. The reversed pair W[k][i] ∧ W[j][k] would mean a path k→i joined to a path j→k, that is j→k→i, reachability from j to i. The two legs must chain from start to intermediate to end, so Warshall uses W[i][k] ∧ W[k][j].

quiz.q: Give one reason a depth-first search from every vertex can beat Warshall's algorithm.
quiz.a: DFS costs O(n(n + m)). On a sparse graph m is much smaller than n², so n(n + m) is much smaller than n³.

quiz.q: State the formula for the symmetric closure of R.

beyond: Not for the exam. Warshall's Boolean matrix loop is the ancestor of bitset transitive closure used in graph databases and compiler call-graph analysis. Modern systems replace the inner OR-AND with word-level bit operations, so 64 matrix entries move per CPU instruction. Search "transitive closure bitset" or "incremental reachability" to see current work. Database engines use transitive closure for recursive SQL queries. Transitive reduction appears in scheduling and in simplifying dependency graphs.
